title: Explicit locks: ReentrantLock, Condition, ReadWriteLock
goal: By the end you can use `ReentrantLock` safely (try/finally, `tryLock`, `lockInterruptibly`), give each kind of waiter its own `Condition`, and use a read-write lock without the upgrade deadlock.

warmup.q: A thread holds the read lock of a `ReentrantReadWriteLock`. It then calls `writeLock().lock()` on the same lock. No other thread touches the lock. What happens?
options: It gets the write lock at once, because it is the only reader
It waits forever: the write lock waits for every reader to leave, and this thread is one of them
It throws `IllegalMonitorStateException`
It gets the write lock and silently drops its read lock
warmup.why: `ReentrantReadWriteLock` does not support upgrading. The write lock needs zero readers, and the thread's own read lock counts. So the thread parks and never wakes. Nothing throws, and, as you'll see in this lesson, a thread dump does not even report it as a deadlock.

steps: Read `TryLockDemo`. A batch thread holds the ledger lock (and a monitor) for 1.5 seconds. `api` uses `tryLock(200 ms)`, `report` uses `lockInterruptibly()`, and `legacy` waits on the monitor with `synchronized`.
Predict the order of the four output lines, and what `getState()` prints for `report` and `legacy`.
Run it. Then change `api` to wait 2 seconds instead of 200 ms and run it again.

The interrupt ends `report`'s wait at once. `legacy` keeps waiting until the batch finishes, and only then sees `interrupted=true`. try.title: Count the wasted wake-ups
steps: Read `WakeupCount`. It moves 20,000 items through a one-slot buffer with 4 producers and 4 consumers. It does this twice: once with one `Condition` and `signalAll()`, once with two `Condition`s and `signal()`.
A wake-up is wasted when a thread wakes, re-checks its `while` condition, and has to wait again. Predict which version wastes more.
Run it twice and compare the counts and the times.

code.title: WakeupCount.java

alt.title: WakeupCount.kt

try.expect: With one condition, tens of thousands of wake-ups are wasted (80,000 to 90,000 in runs here), because every `signalAll()` wakes all seven other threads and most of them go back to sleep. With two conditions, the count drops to hundreds or a few thousand, and the run is several times faster. It isn't zero, because of barging: a running thread can grab the lock and the item before the signalled thread wakes up. That is why the `while` loop stays.

try.title: Upgrade, then downgrade
steps: Run `UpgradeDeadlock`. It tries the upgrade with `tryLock(1, SECONDS)` so it can't hang, then does a downgrade.
Run the Kotlin twin. Its last line puts `write { }` inside `read { }`. Predict: does it hang?
Optional: run the Java one with `-Pargs=hang`. In a second terminal run `jcmd <pid> Thread.print -l` with the printed PID and look at `main`. Stop it with Ctrl+C.

code.title: UpgradeDeadlock.java

alt.title: UpgradeDeadlock.kt

try.expect: `write lock while holding a read lock, after 1 s: false`, then `downgraded: write locked = false, read holds = 1`. The Kotlin `write { }` inside `read { }` does not hang: it prints `write locked = true, read holds = 0`, because Kotlin's `write` lets go of this thread's read locks first. With `-Pargs=hang`, the dump shows `main` parked in `WriteLock.lock` and no deadlock report.

sections.h: StampedLock trades safety rails for speed
sections.body:
Even a read lock writes to shared memory: every reader increments and decrements the lock's count. On a hot path with many cores, that one cache line bounces between them. `StampedLock` (JDK 8) adds a mode with no write at all, the **optimistic read**:

```java
long stamp = lock.tryOptimisticRead();   // 1. no lock, just a version number
long b = bid, a = ask;                   // 2. copy into locals
if (!lock.validate(stamp)) {             // 3. a writer got in: the copies may be torn
    stamp = lock.readLock();             // 4. fall back to a real read lock
    try { b = bid; a = ask; } finally { lock.unlockRead(stamp); }
}
return new Quote(b, a);                  // 5. use the locals only after validate
```

```kotlin
var stamp = lock.tryOptimisticRead()     // 1. no lock, just a version number
var b = bid; var a = ask                 // 2. copy into locals
if (!lock.validate(stamp)) {             // 3. a writer got in: the copies may be torn
    stamp = lock.readLock()              // 4. fall back to a real read lock
    try { b = bid; a = ask } finally { lock.unlockRead(stamp) }
}
return Quote(b, a)                       // 5. use the locals only after validate
```

`tryOptimisticRead()` returns a stamp, a version number of the lock (or 0 if a writer holds it). You read the fields into locals with no lock held. Then `validate(stamp)` asks: did any writer get in since that stamp? If not, your copies are consistent. If yes, you throw them away and read again under a real read lock.

Between steps 2 and 3, the copies can be garbage: a new bid with an old ask. The Javadoc only promises that writes happen-before your reads if a later `validate` returns `true`. So the code between the stamp and the validation must not act on the values. No loops driven by them, no array index, no calls that could throw. Copy, validate, then use.

The price of the speed is a list of things `StampedLock` doesn't do:

- It is **not reentrant**. A thread that holds the write lock and asks for it again waits for itself.
- It has no `Condition`s.
- Stamps are not tied to a thread, and you must pass the right stamp to `unlockRead` or `unlockWrite`.

Use it for a small group of fields that are read on a hot path and written rarely, such as a quote's bid and ask, and only after a profiler shows the read-write lock is the cost. For most code `ReentrantReadWriteLock`, or no lock at all, is the better choice.

try.title: Catch torn reads with validate()
steps: Read `OptimisticRead`. A writer keeps updating a quote, and `ask` is always `bid + 2` once a write is done. The reader counts how many optimistic reads saw a quote where that isn't true.
Predict: will any torn quote get past `validate()`?
Run it. Then delete the `validate` check (treat every optimistic read as good) and count the torn quotes yourself.

code.title: OptimisticRead.java

alt.title: OptimisticRead.kt

try.expect: Thousands of reads fail validation each second, and many of those saw a torn quote (a new bid with an old ask). The last number, torn quotes that passed `validate()`, is always 0. Without the check, those torn quotes would have gone to the caller.

analogy: A `ReentrantLock` is a meeting room with a screen outside. You can queue for the room (`lock`), glance at the screen and leave if it's busy (`tryLock`), queue for at most two minutes (`tryLock(timeout)`), or leave the queue when your phone rings (`lockInterruptibly`). Conditions are separate waiting areas: people waiting for a projector don't get woken when a chair frees up. A read-write lock is a museum gallery: many visitors at once, but the cleaner needs it empty. A visitor can't become the cleaner without walking out first, and if they wait inside for the room to empty, they wait forever. The analogy breaks in one place: a person in the room always leaves eventually. A thread that forgets `unlock()` holds the room for the life of the process.
in_your_world: A Quarkus payment service usually has two lock shapes. One is a per-key lock around a check-and-update, such as a card's daily spend, where `tryLock(50 ms)` lets a request fail fast with a retryable error instead of tying up a worker thread behind a stuck holder. The other is a read-mostly cache, such as FX rates or BIN ranges, refreshed by a scheduled job and read by every request. For the cache, a read-write lock works, but check whether the refresh replaces the whole map. If it does, a `volatile` reference to an immutable map needs no lock at all. In Kotlin services, prefer `withLock`, `read` and `write`, and remember that `write` inside `read` releases the read lock first, so re-check whatever made you decide to write.
mistake: The most common mistake is a `lock()` without a `finally`, or with code between `lock()` and `try` that can throw. One exception on a rare path, a validation error or a timeout from a downstream call, skips the `unlock()`. The lock is now held by a thread that has moved on. Every other thread parks in `ReentrantLock.lock()`, and a dump shows dozens of threads `WAITING (parking)` while `Thread.print -l` names an owner that is idle somewhere else. Nothing ever releases it. The fix is the idiom, every time: `lock()` on the line before `try`, `unlock()` as the first line of `finally`. In Kotlin, use `withLock { }` and the problem can't happen.

compare.title: A read-mostly cache in Java and Kotlin

java.title: Java

kotlin.title: Kotlin

compare.note: The Java version must release the read lock before taking the write lock, or it hangs. The Kotlin version looks like an upgrade, and it doesn't hang, because the standard library's `ReentrantReadWriteLock.write` releases every read lock this thread holds, takes the write lock, and takes the read locks back afterwards. Its documentation warns that this upgrade is not atomic: another thread can write in the gap, so anything you checked before `write` must be checked again inside it. That is why both versions re-check (`computeIfAbsent`, `getOrPut`). Kotlin's helpers remove the ceremony, not the reasoning.

worked.title: A per-card lock that fails fast

steps.say: Authorizations for one card must run one at a time, because each one checks and then updates that card's daily spend. Different cards must not wait for each other. And if one holder gets stuck, other requests for that card should fail fast with a retryable error instead of tying up worker threads. Read the solution and its subgoal labels.

Before reading on, explain to yourself: why does `tryLock` sit outside the `try`, when `unlock()` is inside the `finally`? Answer: if `tryLock` returns `false` or throws `InterruptedException`, this thread doesn't hold the lock. A `finally` that called `unlock()` would throw `IllegalMonitorStateException` and hide the real result. Only the code that runs while you hold the lock goes inside the `try`.

Why not `synchronized (cardId)`? Two `String`s with the same contents are often different objects, so two requests for the same card could each lock their own string and run together. Interned strings go the other way: unrelated code that locks the same literal shares your lock (lesson 4 of this track). And `synchronized` has no timeout. A map of real lock objects avoids all three problems.

One problem remains: the map gains a lock for every card it ever sees, and never shrinks. With millions of cards that is memory you don't get back. Removing entries safely is harder than it looks, because a thread may be about to lock the entry you remove. The usual answer is **lock striping**: a fixed array of locks, chosen by hash.

Two cards that share a stripe now wait for each other. That costs a little throughput and nothing in correctness. If you ever hold two card locks at once, for a transfer between cards, take the stripes in index order, as in lesson 6 of this track, and skip the second lock when both cards land on the same stripe.

lab.title: A buffer with two conditions and a cache that doesn't hang
steps: Run the tests. All eight fail. The five `LockBuffer` tests hit `UnsupportedOperationException`. Two `FxRateCache` tests time out (the upgrade hang), and the snapshot test reports mixed refreshes.

Part 1: write `LockBuffer` with one `ReentrantLock` and two `Condition`s, `notFull` and `notEmpty`. Check the capacity in the constructor. `put` and `take` follow the shape in the second section, with `signal()`.
Write `offer(item, timeout)`: the same as `put`, but wait with `notFull.awaitNanos(remaining)` and return `false` when the time runs out.
Part 2: fix `FxRateCache.rate`. Release the read lock, take the write lock, and re-check before calling the loader, so the loader runs once per pair.
Fix `snapshot` so it reads every pair under one read lock. Run the tests until all eight pass, then twice more.
hints: `awaitNanos` returns the nanoseconds still left (zero or less when time is up). Keep the returned value and pass it to the next `awaitNanos` in the loop.
Use `lock.lockInterruptibly()` at the top of `put`, `take` and `offer`, so an interrupted thread doesn't wait for the lock either. `await()` already throws `InterruptedException` when interrupted.
The cache's `HashMap` is fine as it is: every access to it happens under the read or the write lock. Only the order in which you take the locks is wrong.
lab.done_when: All eight tests in `ExplicitLocksTest` pass, three runs in a row.

drill.title: Two conditions from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. Write a bounded buffer with a `ReentrantLock` and two `Condition`s: `put` waits while full, `take` waits while empty. Check: is every `unlock()` in a `finally`, every `await()` in a `while`, and does each method signal the other side's condition?

alt.title: Kotlin

recap: `ReentrantLock` gives the same exclusion and visibility as `synchronized`, but you release it yourself: `lock()` before `try`, `unlock()` first in `finally`, or Kotlin's `withLock`.
Reach for it when you need `tryLock`, a timeout, `lockInterruptibly`, fairness, or more than one condition.
Each `Condition` is its own wait queue. With one queue per kind of waiter, `signal()` is enough. Still wait in a `while` loop.
A read-write lock lets readers share. Upgrading from read to write hangs forever, and the deadlock detector won't report it. Release, take the write lock, re-check.
`StampedLock` optimistic reads take no lock at all. Copy into locals, `validate`, and only then use the values. It is not reentrant.
Threads waiting on explicit locks show as `WAITING (parking)` in a dump, not `BLOCKED`.

quiz.q: A request handler needs the ledger lock, but must answer 503 if it can't get the lock within 50 ms. Which tool fits?
options: `synchronized (ledger)`
`ledger.lockInterruptibly()`
`ledger.tryLock(50, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)`
A `volatile boolean busy` flag checked before `lock()`
quiz.why: `tryLock` with a timeout waits at most 50 ms and returns `false` if the lock is still taken. `lockInterruptibly` waits without a limit unless someone interrupts the thread. `synchronized` can't time out at all. A `volatile` flag checked before locking is check-then-act: the lock can be taken between the check and the `lock()` call.

quiz.q: Kotlin code: `rw.read { if (cache[k] == null) rw.write { cache[k] = load(k) } }`. Two threads ask for the same missing key. What can happen?
options: Both hang, because a read lock can't be upgraded
`load(k)` can run twice, because `write { }` releases the read lock before it takes the write lock
Nothing bad: `write { }` upgrades atomically
It throws `IllegalMonitorStateException`
quiz.why: Kotlin's `write` releases this thread's read locks, takes the write lock, and restores the read locks after. Both threads can see `null`, both release, and each then loads in turn. It doesn't hang, but it isn't atomic. Re-check inside `write`, for example with `getOrPut`.

quiz.q: From wait, notify and guarded blocks: a teammate merges `notFull` and `notEmpty` into one `Condition changed`, but keeps `changed.signal()` in both `put` and `take`. With several producers and consumers, what can happen?
options: Nothing changes: `signal()` always wakes the right kind of thread
Items are lost
It throws, because two methods can't share one Condition
Everything can stall: a `signal()` meant for a consumer can wake a producer, which waits again, and no one signals the consumers
quiz.why: With one queue for both kinds of waiter, `signal()` may pick the wrong kind. That thread re-checks, waits again, and the signal is gone. It is the same lost wake-up that made the one-monitor buffer need `notifyAll()`. With one condition, use `signalAll()`; with two, `signal()` is fine.

quiz.q: With `StampedLock`, you call `tryOptimisticRead()` and copy `bid` and `ask` into locals. What must happen before you use them?
options: Call `validate(stamp)`; if it returns false, read them again under `readLock()`
Nothing: the stamp guarantees a consistent read
Call `unlockRead(stamp)`
Call `tryConvertToWriteLock(stamp)`
quiz.why: An optimistic read takes no lock, so a writer can change the fields while you copy them. `validate` tells you whether a writer got in since the stamp. Only after it returns `true` are the copies known to be consistent. There is nothing to release, because nothing was locked.

quiz.q: A dump shows 40 worker threads `WAITING (parking)` in `ReentrantLock.lock()`. `Thread.print -l` says the lock is owned by `kafka-consumer-3`, whose stack shows it idle inside `poll()`. What is the most likely bug?
options: A deadlock between the workers
The lock is unfair, so the workers are starving
A code path in the consumer took the lock and left without `unlock()`, for example on an exception with no `finally`
`poll()` holds the lock internally
quiz.why: The owner isn't waiting for anything you'd expect, and it isn't in the critical section. It has moved on while still holding the lock, which happens when an exception or an early return skips the release. An unfair lock would still hand over now and then, and a deadlock needs the owner to wait for a lock too.

flashcards.front: Where do `lock()` and `unlock()` go relative to `try`/`finally`?
flashcards.back: `lock()` on the line right before `try`. `unlock()` as the first statement of `finally`. In Kotlin, `lock.withLock { }` does both.

flashcards.front: What does `lock.tryLock(50, MILLISECONDS)` do when another thread holds the lock?
flashcards.back: It waits up to 50 ms. It returns `true` (and you hold the lock) if it got it in time, `false` otherwise. It throws `InterruptedException` if interrupted while waiting.

flashcards.front: A thread waits in `lockInterruptibly()` and another thread interrupts it. What happens? And for a thread waiting to enter `synchronized`?
flashcards.back: `lockInterruptibly()` gives up at once with `InterruptedException`. The `synchronized` waiter keeps waiting until it gets the monitor; it only sees its interrupt flag afterwards.

flashcards.front: Why can a bounded buffer with `notFull` and `notEmpty` conditions use `signal()` instead of `signalAll()`?
flashcards.back: Each condition has only one kind of waiter, and one change (one item in, or one slot free) lets exactly one of them proceed.

flashcards.front: A thread holding the read lock of a `ReentrantReadWriteLock` calls `writeLock().lock()`. What happens?
flashcards.back: It waits forever. The write lock waits for every reader to leave, including this thread. Release the read lock first, then re-check under the write lock.

flashcards.front: After `long s = lock.tryOptimisticRead()` and copying fields into locals, what must you do?
flashcards.back: Call `lock.validate(s)`. If it returns false, a writer got in: read the fields again under `lock.readLock()`.

flashcards.front: In Kotlin, what does `rw.write { }` do when called inside `rw.read { }`?
flashcards.back: It releases this thread's read locks, takes the write lock, and restores the read locks afterwards. It doesn't hang, but it isn't atomic: re-check inside the block.

terms.plain: An explicit lock with the same rules as `synchronized`, plus `tryLock`, timeouts, interruptible waits, fairness and conditions.
How many times the owning thread has taken a reentrant lock. It must release it as many times.
A wait queue tied to a lock. `await()` releases the lock and waits; `signal()` wakes one waiter.
A lock that hands over to the longest-waiting thread instead of letting new arrivals barge in.
A pair of locks: many threads may hold the read lock together; the write lock is exclusive.
Going from a read lock to a write lock while still holding the read lock. `ReentrantReadWriteLock` hangs if you try.
A `StampedLock` read that takes no lock and checks afterwards, with `validate`, that no writer got in.

explain_back.prompt: A teammate asks: "Should we replace all our `synchronized` blocks with `ReentrantLock`? I heard it's faster." Explain what you would tell them.
explain_back.answer: Not by default. Both give the same mutual exclusion and visibility, and on current JDKs their speed is similar for ordinary critical sections. `synchronized` can't leak: it releases on every exit. With `ReentrantLock` you must release in a `finally`, and one missed path holds the lock forever. I'd switch only where we need something `synchronized` can't do: give up after a timeout with `tryLock`, let an interrupt cancel the wait with `lockInterruptibly`, use a fair lock, or have separate conditions for different kinds of waiters. For read-mostly data I'd look at a read-write lock, or better, an immutable snapshot behind a `volatile` reference.

deeper.body:
`ReentrantLock`, `ReentrantReadWriteLock`, `Semaphore` and `CountDownLatch` are all built on one class, `AbstractQueuedSynchronizer` (AQS). It keeps one `int` of state and a queue of waiting threads. For `ReentrantLock` the state is the hold count; for a semaphore it is the number of permits left; for a latch it is the count. A thread that can't proceed joins the queue and parks with `LockSupport.park`. That is why it shows as `WAITING` in a dump, with a line like `parking to wait for <0x...> (a java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantLock$NonfairSync)`. A release unparks the next thread in the queue.

In non-fair mode, the default, a thread that arrives just as the lock is released can take it before the queued thread wakes. That is barging, and it is why the two-condition buffer in the second Try it still wasted some wake-ups. It is also why non-fair locks have much higher throughput: waking a parked thread takes microseconds, and a running thread can take and release the lock many times in that gap. Fair mode closes the gap and pays the wake-up cost on every hand-off. Even on a fair lock, the untimed `tryLock()` barges: its Javadoc says it does not honor the fairness setting.

`ReentrantReadWriteLock` splits its 32-bit state into two 16-bit halves, one for read holds and one for write holds. That is why its Javadoc caps it at 65,535 recursive write locks and 65,535 read locks.

`StampedLock` also has `tryConvertToWriteLock(stamp)`, which upgrades a read or optimistic stamp to a write stamp if no other thread is in the way, and returns 0 if it can't. It is the only upgrade in the JDK's locks, and it can fail, so you still need the fallback path.

If you ever build your own synchronizer, subclass AQS and implement `tryAcquire` and `tryRelease`; its Javadoc has a small `Mutex` example. First check `java.util.concurrent` for one that already exists. Lesson 10 of this track covers the common ones.
